assumptions.summary: Calm sea is smooth and produces specular reflection.
A conservative best available frequency of 20 MHz represents the 3-30 MHz band.
Emission and reception directional factors are fixed at one.
The transmitted wave is circularly polarized.
Only wave frequency and height represent rough sea state, both driven by wind.
Dry ground is smooth and mountainous terrain is represented by a typical double-edged peak plus foliage.
The antenna moves with the vessel and wind-wave heave/roll/pitch summarize six degrees of freedom.
The ionosphere consists of thin uniform-density sheets and endpoint frequencies bound a common coverage region.

contributions.summary: The paper organizes one prompt into a reusable ocean-baseline -> terrain-transfer -> moving-receiver sequence.
An additive link budget makes atmospheric and surface stages independently replaceable.
Sea material properties are estimated before polarization-specific Fresnel reflection.
A smooth interface is extended through wind spectrum, height, roughness, and curvature rather than rebuilt.
Common incident power cancels so the rough/smooth effect is expressed through a correction-factor ratio.
The 10-dB usability condition converts continuous loss into a maximum hop count.
Mountain loss is decomposed into two-edge diffraction, coupling, and foliage absorption.
One four-class chart supports a direct environment ranking.
Ship sway is added only to the path region where the paper considers it material.
A technical workflow is compressed into a Communications Magazine-style synopsis.

independent_extensions.summary: Rebuild the link budget with unit-consistent positive attenuation, authoritative lookup tables, and a complete per-hop power ledger.
Calibrate complex sea permittivity against temperature, salinity, frequency, and measured reflection magnitude/phase.
Generate rough surfaces from a documented directional spectrum with seed, discretization, shadowing, and Monte Carlo convergence.
Publish a recursive multi-hop SNR simulator with surface sequence, noise bandwidth units, intermediate values, and threshold sensitivity.

models.summary: The paper decomposes total skywave loss, uses free-space spreading and a solar/geomagnetic absorption relation, selects one East China Sea scenario, and reports 97.4597 dB total loss and 0.43248 mW incident power.
The paper combines a complex-permittivity relation with two CCIR-style piecewise fits and evaluates them at 20 MHz as epsilon_r=70, sigma=5.0, and printed epsilon=70+4500i.
Using complex sea permittivity and grazing angle, the paper defines two polarization coefficients and plots power reflection versus angle.
The paper uses a PM spectrum and a wind-height relation, forms a Miller-Brown correction with a Bessel function, adds a curvature factor, and scales both smooth polarization coefficients.
The paper averages squared horizontal/vertical coefficients for circular polarization, cancels the common incident power, derives a rho-squared ratio, and reports smooth/rough powers.
The paper defines received field strength, atmospheric-noise field strength, and a combined SNR expression, then reports eight 400-km hops from the rough-sea first reflection.
The paper sets dry-earth complex permittivity to 4, reuses the Fresnel and transmission-loss interface, and reports 9.1133 dB reflection loss.
The paper reduces a typical double-edged peak to two single-edge terms, adds a geometry correction and linear foliage loss, then uses one illustrative terrain scenario.
The paper presents a four-bar reflection-loss chart, pairs it with land hop counts, and concludes that sea surfaces better support shortwave skywave transmission.
The paper reduces six-degree ship motion to heave, roll, and pitch, then cites a maximum sway-angle relation because measured vessel motion is unavailable.
The Earth-curved path is partitioned into A, B, and C; segment A uses dual path plus sway, B uses direct path, and C is a shadow zone. The paper reports 1.5 dB sway loss.

The paper treats the ionosphere as parallel refractive sheets, applies a Snell invariant and a path integral, takes the difference between high/low-frequency paths, and reports 840 km coverage and 15.12 hours at 30 knots.
Figures 11-12 show curve families labeled by time from 0 to 22 hours; the paper interprets angle/SNR as time-sensitive and ionospheric loss as weakly time-sensitive.

results_trace.summary: The selected one-hop scenario reports 97.4597 dB loss.
The 100-W source is reported to reach the sea with 0.43248 mW.
At 20 MHz the paper reports epsilon_r=70, sigma=5.0, and complex permittivity 70+4500i.
For the selected wind/angle/wavelength scenario rho is reported as 0.8043.
The body reports smooth P1=0.4378 mW and rough P2=0.2832 mW, with ratio 0.64689849.
The maximum usable count is reported as eight 400-km hops.
Smooth dry terrain reflection loss is reported as 9.1133 dB.
The paper reports three hops for smooth ground and two for mountainous terrain.
Figure 7 reports 12.1084, 9.1133, 2.855, and 0.9637 dB for mountain, smooth ground, turbulent sea, and calm sea.
One sending/receiving process is assigned a 1.5-dB sway penalty.
The source reports an 840-km signal-coverage width and 15.12-hour communication time at 30 knots.
The paper characterizes SNR/grazing response as time-sensitive and ionospheric loss as weakly time-sensitive.

weaknesses.summary: A red commercial/template watermark appears on every rendered page, and internal page totals alternate among 22 and 24 while the PDF has 25 physical pages; document provenance and pagination are not clean.
The Summary assigns 0.4378 mW to rough sea and 0.2832 mW to smooth sea, while the body assigns those values in the opposite order.
The magazine synopsis repeats the Summary's rough/smooth power reversal rather than the body's stated P1/P2 ownership.
The reported smooth reflected power 0.4378 mW exceeds the reported incident power 0.43248 mW, so the coefficient/power convention fails a basic energy check.
Equation 7 prints L_b=10 log10(P_r/P_t), which is negative for attenuation; the usual positive loss direction is 10 log10(P_t/P_r).
Equation 3 is introduced as ionospheric absorption L_i but visually labels the left side L_bf, already owned by free-space loss.
Solar-geometry Equation 6 and the chosen date/location do not publish all intermediate coordinates, lookup values, angle conventions, or a reproducible numeric calculation.
The 1.24-MHz magnetic-frequency term and extra system loss are described as lookup values but the data sheet, interpolation, and actual Y_p value are absent.
Equation 8's i60 lambda sigma convention and the result 70+4500i lack a unit/sign convention and temperature/salinity conditions.
The relative-permittivity piecewise relation has no printed Equation 9 label, breaking the otherwise sequential Equation 1-33 reference chain.
Equation 10 repeats u in both first- and second-order denominator terms while defining v but not using it; the conductivity fit cannot be trusted without its source form.
Equations 18-20 square complex Fresnel coefficients directly rather than explicitly using magnitude squared, leaving the power calculation physically ambiguous.
The choice theta=45 degrees is justified only by visual inspection that reflection changes little from 45-90 degrees; no quantified approximation error or polarization-specific sensitivity is given.
The PM spectrum is called a 'Neutron spectrum', and references 6-7 cited near the wave-height model are unrelated power-electronics papers rather than ocean-wave sources.
The same wind-speed-to-wave-height explanatory paragraph is duplicated verbatim, adding no evidence and obscuring editorial control.
The assumptions dismiss shadowing as inapplicable, but the rough-sea section states wavelength and wave height are comparable and shadowing may occur before ignoring it again.
Equation 16 does not clearly define G2 or phi in the prose, and the sentence identifying effective Earth radius is grammatically missing its symbol.
The paper defines curvature-adjusted rho-prime=rho D, but Equation 17 scales Fresnel coefficients by rho rather than rho-prime, apparently dropping the curvature correction.
Equation 20 changes the rough reflected-power symbol from P2 to undefined P3, so the derived ratio is not symbolically closed.
The noise-bandwidth B is assigned '6 dB' although Equation 22 requires a bandwidth before logarithm; transmitter power also shifts between W and kW without a full unit ledger.
The reported maximum of eight hops has no per-hop power/SNR recurrence, intermediate table, surface sequence, code, or stopping trace.
The 9.1133-dB smooth-ground loss and three-hop result are asserted from inherited Fresnel formulas without showing ground conductivity, coefficient, loss conversion, or SNR calculation.
The terrain example uses foliage attenuation a_L=0.8 even though the immediately stated usual range is 0.01-0.1 dB/m.
The mountainous 12.1084-dB loss and two-hop result have no component ledger for L1, L2, Lc, foliage loss, reflection loss, or the resulting SNR.
Figure 7 compares four reflection-loss bars, but the prose also claims transmission-distance and hop superiority without common uncertainty, route geometry, or measured validation.
Equation 29 is typographically ambiguous and supplies no H_max, sea wavelength, evaluated sway angle, vessel geometry, or measured motion.
The Figure 9 paragraph incorrectly refers to Figure 8; C_DP and C_RP, segment boundaries, and the entire segment-C shadow model are undefined.
Equations 30-31 and the 1.5-dB sway result lack a unit derivation, coefficient values, distance dependence, and numerical trace.
Equation 33 leaves refractive-index profile, r_b/r_t bounds, endpoint frequencies, quadrature method, and path evaluations undefined, so the 840-km coverage width is not reproducible.

The time sweep shows only one scenario and tiny ionospheric-loss differences, yet the paper claims the model is suitable 'for anytime', that grazing incidence is very sensitive, and that each parameter received error/sensitivity analysis without measured validation.

writing_logic.summary: HF relevance -> six tasks -> assumptions/notation -> loss budget -> smooth sea material/Fresnel baseline -> roughness and curvature -> controlled power ratio -> SNR hop threshold -> smooth/mountain land transfer -> four-surface ranking -> ship sway and segmented path -> frequency coverage time -> time sensitivity -> strengths/weaknesses -> magazine synopsis.

One HF skywave hop can be represented by an explicit loss budget and incident-power handoff. Decompose aggregate loss by physical cause. Compute free-space and ionospheric components. Set one time-location-frequency scenario. Convert total loss from a 100-W source to sea-surface incident power. All sea-surface comparisons consume one common first-hop input.

Smooth-sea reflection follows from material properties before surface-state perturbations are added. Fit relative permittivity and conductivity from frequency. Form complex sea permittivity. Compute horizontal and vertical Fresnel coefficients. Average them for circular polarization. The smooth surface becomes a controlled baseline rather than a separate ad hoc result.

Wind modifies reflection through a traceable spectrum-height-roughness chain. Represent wave frequencies with a PM spectrum. Map wind speed to RMS height. Build a dimensionless roughness. Apply local and curvature corrections. Scale smooth coefficients. The rough/smooth power ratio is attributed to rho squared.

A usable-hop limit can be framed as a repeated SNR threshold decision. Compute received field strength. Compute atmospheric noise. Combine them into SNR. Repeat loss updates until SNR falls below 10 dB. The paper reports eight 400-km hops for the sea scenario.

The sea model can be transferred to land by replacing material properties and adding terrain mechanisms. Reuse Fresnel reflection for dry smooth ground. Reduce mountains to two diffraction edges. Add a coupling correction. Add foliage attenuation. Apply the same hop criterion. Four surfaces can be ranked by loss and reported hop reach.

A four-surface comparison turns component models into a terrain decision. Collect mountain and smooth-ground losses. Collect turbulent- and calm-sea losses. Plot all four on one axis. Interpret land/sea and rough/smooth differences. The paper recommends sea propagation as the more favorable shortwave environment.

Receiver motion can be added through a bounded angle and segment-specific path penalty. Reduce vessel six-DOF motion to heave, roll, and pitch. Estimate a maximum sway angle. Partition the curved-Earth path into A/B/C. Apply dual-path sway only in segment A. The static ocean model becomes a moving-vessel receiver model with a reported 1.5-dB penalty.

Frequency-dependent ionospheric paths create a coverage envelope that can be converted into communication time. Model the ionosphere as refractive sheets. Apply the Snell invariant. Integrate high- and low-frequency paths. Take their distance difference. Divide by vessel speed and inspect time sensitivity. The paper reports 840 km and 15.12 hours before compressing results for a maritime audience.
